problem.heading:
Is water present?
Is it accumulating? What changed?
problem.intro: A plumbing leak, condensate problem and basement ingress need different evidence. Design the measurement set around likely sources and vulnerable assets.

cards.title: Water reaches valuable assets
cards.body: Cooling connections, plumbing and roof or ground ingress can expose equipment and stored material. Contact detection belongs on a plausible water path, with access for inspection.

cards.title: Collection points fill between visits
cards.body: A sump or drainage vessel can accumulate water beyond the contact point. A suitable level record adds the depth and trend needed for the maintenance review.

cards.title: Moisture persists after the event
cards.body: Air humidity and cold surfaces can complicate recovery or a condensation investigation. These measurements add context; a dry detector alone does not describe the condition of building materials.

problem.takeaway: Use the right observation for the question: contact for presence, level for accumulation and environmental measurements for moisture context.

focus.heading:
Follow the water path.
Build the response around it.
focus.intro: Map likely sources first. Then choose contact, level and environmental points that support distinct maintenance decisions.

stages.title: Survey the exposure
stages.body: Identify water services, ingress paths, floor levels, drains and vulnerable equipment or contents.

stages.title: Select complementary observations
stages.body: Specify contact detection on plausible paths, level at collection points and environmental context where needed.

stages.title: Test the event and permitted action
stages.body: Verify the water event and duty notification. Where control is included, check the command, actual valve or pump feedback and local override.

stages.title: Restore and review
stages.body: After action, check the sensing arrangement and review recurring events with the site maintenance record.

focus.note: Water must reach the monitored contact point. Coverage, alert timing and response access are defined and tested for the actual site.
focus.detailTitle: Distinguish water detection from a moisture assessment
focus.detail: A contact detector reports liquid at its sensing location; level adds depth relative to a reference. Air humidity and surface temperature can support a condensation investigation when measured at relevant positions. They do not identify every source or measure retained moisture within materials. Use an appropriate building or contents assessment where drying is the decision. Keep functional tests safe for electrical equipment and vulnerable stored items.

faq.q: What is included in Smart Water Leak Monitoring?
faq.a: Combine H Series point water detection with suitable collection-level measurements and available pump or valve feedback. Add ambient or surface measurements when condensation or recovery is the concern. A commissioned Hitelecom controller can provide permitted remote or condition-based actions. The sensing, control interface, feedback and response workflow are selected for the installation.

faq.q: How is this different from Smart Water Monitoring?
faq.a: This solution focuses on water reaching vulnerable buildings, equipment or contents, and the facilities response. Smart Water Monitoring focuses on water-system operation, including level, conveyance and supply conditions. A sump can appear in either plan, but its measurement should serve a clearly defined operating question.

faq.q: Can humidity detect a leak or prove that a room is dry?
faq.a: No. Relative humidity describes moisture in the air, while contact detection observes liquid at a sensing point. Neither proves that all surfaces, materials or contents are dry. Use environmental data as supporting context and arrange an appropriate moisture or contents assessment when the recovery decision requires it.

faq.q: How are detection points and level sensors positioned?
faq.a: Survey likely sources, water paths, floor levels, drains and collection points. Select accessible contact locations and a suitable level reference, then confirm the supplied arrangement with an approved test. One dry contact point cannot establish that the whole room is dry, so coverage must be designed around the actual layout.

faq.q: Does the system automatically shut a valve or start a pump?
faq.a: It can include a permitted valve or pump action through a suitably configured HD20 controller or documented compatible interface. Define the output electrical type, load-control circuit, local priority and independent feedback. Test command acceptance, actual equipment response and power or communication loss. The water sensor alone does not operate the equipment, and existing plant protection remains active.

faq.q: What should happen after a water event?
faq.a: Follow the site procedure to address the source and affected area safely. Then inspect and clean the sensing arrangement, verify its reported recovery and document the outcome. Review repeated events with drainage, cleaning and service records. Assess retained moisture or damaged contents separately where the recovery plan requires it.

faq.q: Can we use sensing cable instead of individual point probes?
faq.a: Specify cable coverage when long pipe routes, raised floors or room perimeters require it. The published H300-WL002A reference is a two-pin point-sensing model; a compatible sensing cable and detector / interface must be confirmed separately. Establish whether the requirement is one wet-zone indication or distance-to-leak locating, then test the full installed route.

faq.q: Will the same sensor detect oil, solvent or every coolant?
faq.a: Do not assume so. Confirm the actual water, condensate, coolant mixture, conductivity and cleaning conditions. Oil and solvents can require a different sensing principle and suitable equipment approvals. Test the supplied sensing arrangement with an approved representative liquid before treating it as a dependable point in the response workflow.
